title: Decrease lock contention and syscall wakeups in request dispatch path
author: Asha Verma
description: Motivation: production traces and Flame graphs showed that the CPU-side request dispatch path hits significant overhead from short critical sections, frequent futex/eventfd wakeups, and cross-core thread migration. This PR reduces end-to-end per-request CPU overhead by sharding the dispatch queues, replacing a global mutex with per-shard MPSC ring buffers and a lightweight seqlock on metadata, and batching wakeups to the worker pool to avoid syscalls on hot paths. Approach: 1) Introduce DispatchShard and MPSCRingBuffer to avoid a single global lock; each shard pins to a CPU core group and owns its queue. 2) Move small serializing work (request header packing and priority calculation) out of the hot path and into the dispatch handoff where it can be done in bulk for a batch of requests. 3) Replace eventfd notifications with a coalescing eventfd + in-process condition that minimizes kernel wakeups for bursty traffic. 4) Thread pool: add optional core-affinity policy and a lightweight back-off so workers avoid repeated cross-socket steal attempts. 5) Add a non-blocking fast-path for cache hits: if KV-cache metadata indicates a warm key, the dispatcher attaches a KV pointer and avoids extra serialization. The description below contains the checklist and results. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for ring buffer and shard lifecycle - [x] Synthetic perf benchmark (p95 CPU reduction) - [x] Integration test against continuous batching harness - [x] Add docs for affinity config - [x] Manual canary (internal) Results: Microbenchmarks (local, 8-core c6i-like VM): p50 latency unchanged, p95 latency reduced by ~18%, CPU cycles per 1k requests reduced by ~22%, context-switch rate reduced by ~41% under synthetic burst load. Production canary (20% of traffic in us-west-2, 72h): 17% lower CPU usage on dispatch-heavy routes, no errors introduced, one flaky integration test retried in CI. Rollout: squash-merge to main, will be included in next minor release unless a hotfix is required. Rollback plan: revert the feature flag for shard dispatch or fall back to the previous global queue. Notes: this PR focuses exclusively on CPU-side dispatch and does not modify kernel-level kernels or model execution paths; it is complementary to ongoing batching/kernel work in other PRs.

discussion: Miguel Santos (reviewer): The sharding approach looks good; did you validate skewed routing where a single shard gets overloaded? Please add a counter and fallback to cross-shard steal.
Asha Verma (author): Added cross-shard steal in thread_pool.cc and a metric shard_imbalance_count. When imbalance > 1000 in 10s we allow limited stealing (configurable).
Priya Kapoor (reviewer): Concern about memory reclamation for ring buffer nodes; is there an ABA risk?
Asha Verma (author): Ring uses index-based slots with epoch-counter to avoid ABA; unit tests added to simulate wrap-around. See mpsc_ring_buffer.cc for details.
Jonah Lee (approver): Verified benchmarks and CI artifacts. Approving — good improvement for dispatch-heavy routes.

release_notes: Reduced CPU overhead in request dispatch: per-shard queues and coalesced wakeups reduce CPU and context switches for bursty workloads; configurable affinity policy for the worker pool.
risk_impact: Low-to-medium: guarded by feature flag; regressions limited to dispatch path. Possible increased memory footprint due to per-shard queues.
testing_notes: Included microbench harness (tests/perf/dispatch_bench.cc) and integration run against continuous-batching canary. Load tests ran for 72h at 20% traffic. Unit tests cover ring buffer edge cases.
motivation: Observed high futex/syscall rate and short critical sections creating CPU overhead that limited throughput and increased cost for small inference requests. This PR addresses those issues without changing model execution.
